58.t: Breathing and playing inside the lip
58.s: Punch breathes every other bar, explains why one trumpet needed no shared breathing, and how he fixed playing inside his lip.
58.ch: Trumpet technique: breath, lip and effects
58.q: Yeah. Then I played with a band named Hughie Swift from Chicago, where you played the, if you're playing, you know, brass all together, everybody breathed the same way. Just at the same time.

58.t: Holding a note through a twelve-bar blues chorus
58.s: Punch says he could hold a note for a chorus on trumpet, an idea from Joe Howard, unlike clarinetists.
58.q: Right here on his tongue. I remember we used to play, uh, the blues and I'd hold a note like I heard that client, they'd play a hold on it on that blues. I had a record there where a guy holds a note on the planet. I don't get his name. He's a white boy. No, I don't. Maybe he's white. I don't know.

58.ch: Making up numbers, bop and technique

But that got to get solid again see. I can hit the note but when I get ready to come down, it messes up. I'll tell you why, because I just…

58.q: Yeah I have to do that like that. That looks clumsy. Now Lee Collin, he played just like this. I don't see how I can get his fingers out of the way. He plays right... Yeah, just like that. What part of the hand do you call that? It seems right, I don't know how he can do that. And get his hand out…

58.s: Punch and Allen discuss how vibrato, growl and flutter tongue are made, and Punch can no longer growl.
58.ch: Trumpet technique: breath, lip and effects
58.q: Well, I don't do it now, but I used to, but I went from the lip. But some people do it from the throat now, don't they? From the throat.

58.s: Punch demonstrates how Buddy Petit, Celestin and Young Kid Punch placed the horn on the lip.

58.q: Well, Buddy Petit lived way on the side here. On his right side? Right side, yeah. Right side. Right there. Just like that. That's where he played. And if anybody noticed Pop Silistan, he put this part in front, but the bottom part around here. That's what he used to play like. Like that.

101.s: Brower's conversation with Faddis and a young trumpeter; Terry denies trombone influence.

101.s: Terry credits buzzing without the horn for keeping his chops.

825.s: Metoyer did not push the non-pressure system on young Ernie, wanting him to build lip muscle. He used it himself when tired from jitney dances and favored playing with moist lips.
825.q: Well, no. He didn't actually stress to me about the non-pressure system of playing. Even when he started me on double-tonging and triple-tonging, he wanted me to use... By me being so young, he wanted me to build the muscles up in my lips. See, that was the general idea. The non-pressure system,…

825.t: Playing in the center of the mouth
825.s: Metoyer insisted on playing from the center of the lips and breathing from the stomach to build even muscle.
825.q: Well, no, he didn't. He let me choose whatever he figured would fit my armature better, you know. He was very particular of me trying to play in the center of my mouth.

825.t: Standing to play and the sandwich anecdote
825.s: The men tell how Metoyer would eat a sandwich between choruses. They talk about trumpeters who stand to play, including Bunk Johnson, and Metoyer's duets with Ernie.
825.q: I know you've heard of it. Out on the lake shore there, he used to play several jobs with old man Dave Perkins. Oh yeah, it's a new band. Yeah, out on the lake. And I know he used to play a job with them and he would be standing up, just like to do

825.t: Teeth, false teeth and trumpet players
825.s: Metoyer stressed caring for teeth. The men discuss trumpeters with false teeth, including Bunk Johnson and Gilbert Young, and Young's jitney work.
825.q: Well, yeah, let you take good care of your teeth, you see. And one thing he knows is, you know, if they're not projecting out in a way like that, that kind of, you know, way hurts you. If you're in a way that projecting teeth, they couldn't make no good trumpet players.

825.s: Metoyer taught taking breaths at the ends of bars and using the stomach. He always stood up to play, even on jitney dances.
825.q: Well, yeah, see, in fact, he taught me from the whole note of breathing at the end of each bar, if you can, that's where you take your breath. Unless you have a break in between the bar where you can take a breath and you're going to have a tie over to the next bar to keep you from turning that tie…

825.t: First trumpet, mouthpiece and lower-lip placement
825.s: Ernie began in 1927 on a silver Conn 22B with a cushion-rim mouthpiece. He explains why the mouthpiece sits more on the lower lip, a method he says came from the Arban tradition.
825.q: No, my mouthpiece was always cushioned rim. I started with it. My first trumpet was a Kahn 22B. It was a Silver Kahn 22B Kahn at that time.

508.t: Vibrato borrowed from opera and what classical saxophone allows
508.s: Not using vibrato at moments of tension came from listening to opera, and he uses the same idea in jazz.
508.q: I don’t think that the music itself gives a damn, as long as it sounds classical. The idea is not to come in and play Louis Armstrong growls in the middle of it. The idea is to use the sound – all these sounds. Like I use all the sounds that I have in my head. In terms of pacing, in terms of tone,…

508.t: Daily practice and refusing a smaller mouthpiece for speed
508.s: He practices hard passages as etudes and keeps his tenor tone instead of using a smaller mouthpiece.
508.q: Practicing. Playing these pieces. And when you get to the parts of the pieces that are really difficult, you stop and you turn them into little etudes and you play them over and over, and over and over again. And how it helps in jazz is that many times in the past when I had…my imagination will…

508.t: Tone and sound production in classical versus jazz saxophone
508.s: You play a style accurately only by listening to it; he has heard classical records since high school and the heavy jazz sound has faded.
508.q: Well, it’s really a lot simpler than it seems, but I guess it’s also harder than it sounds. But, you are not going to be able to accurately play styles of music if you don’t listen to those musics. And so many musicians, so many people who choose to become musicians are the kind of people that rely…

508.s: Milhaud recreated the sound of jazz rather than imitating it; on Solitude his classical vibrato instinct made the tenor sound like an alto.

93.t: Four and a half years with Buck and Bubbles and training on wooden floors
93.s: They spent four and a half years in the act, three of them trained by Bubbles on wooden floors at Rockland Palace, the Hotcha Club and Renaissance Ballroom.

93.q: Well, we were with the Buck and Bubbles act for four and a half years. And we were never allowed to be away from Mr. Bubbles -- Nat Nazarrq. 235.t: Dental work and saxophone players' mouths

149.t: Filing down a mouthpiece to reach high notes
149.s: Hearing a Lunceford trumpeter, he shaved an old mouthpiece wider and shallower until he could hit the notes.
149.q: Well, I heard Steve, [Tommy Stevenson] Ben Stevens. I think he was playing trumpet with Jimmy Lunceford. And, I tried it with the mouthpiece that I had. You know, a regular mouthpiece, and I couldn't make it.

124.s: Gunable, a top East Coast teacher, had pupils build embouchure strength by blowing the mouthpiece alone, which McRae credits for his tone.
124.ch: Philadelphia and the McRae Brothers Band, 1908-1929
124.q: Well, the fellow I just -- I don't know if anybody know this fellow's name, Mike Gunable. He was one of the top teachers in the East.

455.s: Budd's five-minute held note astonishes Haitians, and he explains circular breathing, as Clark Terry and Buster Bailey also did.
455.ch: Cab Calloway, Haiti and Sarah Vaughan
455.q: And I never will forget, I was written up in every Haitian newspaper, front page news, because I used the circular breathing thing, and I held a note for about five minutes, and they wanted to know what God did I have in New York that could give me all of this breath, you know.
